newsitem.title: UK: Sinn Fein tells Britain to leave N.Ireland.
newsitem.headline: Sinn Fein tells Britain to leave N.Ireland.

text.p: Sinn Fein President Gerry Adams held his first talks with Britain's new Northern Ireland Secretary, Mo Mowlam, on Wednesday and told her to oversee the end of British rule in Northern Ireland.

"Sinn Fein enters negotiations as an Irish Republican party seeking to promote the broad nationalist objective of an end to British rule in Ireland," Adams told Mowlam at their first meeting since his IRA guerrilla allies called a July 20 truce.
He said that "while I welcome Mo Mowlam as the first woman British Secretary of State for Northern Ireland, I hope she will be the last."

Adams used the two-hour talks to set out the agenda he wants discussed if Sinn Fein is admitted to Anglo-Irish peace talks in September after being banned for years because of the IRA's 28-year war against British rule.
Mowlam said it would be -- providing the IRA stuck by its latest ceasefire "in word and deed". She said she wanted the talks to include all the province's rival pro-British and pro-Irish parties.
Adams, with convicted IRA gun-runner Martin Ferris in his team, raised key issues he wants on the talks' agenda, over which he and successive British governments have been widely at odds.
He urged Britain's new Labour government to persuade Northern Ireland's Protestant unionist majority to stop clinging to British rule and be part of a re-united Ireland.

He said it should "play a crucial and constructive role in persuading unionists to reach a democratic agreement on the issue of Irish national reunification with the rest of the people of this island and to encourage, facilitate and enable such agreement."

Britain and its Irish partners in a three-year peace process say Northern Ireland's British status cannot change until a majority of its 1.5 million people, 60 percent Protestant and 40 percent Catholic at present, want it.

But Adams, rehearsing arguments he will bring to the conference table in September, said Northern Ireland was an "illegal statelet" and its future should be decided by the overwhelmingly Roman Catholic population of the entire island of Ireland.
Mowlam said in remarks released to the media that the British government wanted both the IRA and pro-British loyalist guerrilla groups to surrender their weapons as talks progressed.
But Adams and his chief negotiator, Martin McGuinness, said that the IRA, in statements to the media, had made clear it will give up nothing until a final settlement is reached.
The issue is crucial because Northern Ireland's main Protestant group, the Ulster Unionist Party led by David Trimble, wants Britain to force the IRA to disarm during, not after, the talks.
It fears that the IRA will return to a campaign of bombing and killing if a united Ireland is not part of a final settlement to a conflict that has killed 3,200 in 28 years.

Trimble is canvassing UUP members to see whether they want him to remain at the negotiating table if the IRA will not disarm. Two smaller unionist parties have already walked out of the talks altogether over the arms decommissioning proposals.
The IRA has enough automatic rifles to arm a battalion, and tonnes of semtex plastic explosive. Many of its weapons date back to the 1980s, when they were smuggled in by activists like Ferris.
Ferris was convicted of IRA membership in 1984 and jailed for 10 years for attempting to smuggle tonnes of arms into Ireland from the United States on board the Marita Ann ship.
"My presence here is no different to that of many others looking to bring peace and justice in our country," Ferris told reporters at the end of the talks.
